title: DCPSC Order No. 22893 (2026-06-30) — The Public Service Commission of the District of Columbia, in Formal Case No. 1176, by Order No. 22893, dated June 30, 2026, granted, in part, and denied, in pa
description: The Public Service Commission of the District of Columbia, in Formal Case No. 1176, by Order No. 22893, dated June 30, 2026, granted, in part, and denied, in part, the Motion for Enlargement of Time of the Office of the People’s Counsel for the District of Columbia, the District of Columbia Government, and the Apartment and Office Building Association of Metropolitan Washington. The deadline for filing post-hearing briefs is extended to November 4, 2026.

I.
INTRODUCTION
1.
By this Order, the Public Service Commission of the District of Columbia
(“Commission”) grants, in part, and denies, in part, the Motion for Enlargement of Time of the 
Office of the People’s Counsel for the District of Columbia (“OPC” or “Office”), the District of 
Columbia Government (“DCG”), and the Apartment and Office Building Association of 
Metropolitan Washington (“AOBA”) (collectively, the “Joint Movants”).1 The deadline for filing 
post-hearing briefs is extended to November 4, 2026. 
II.
BACKGROUND
2.
On April 13, 2023, the Potomac Electric Power Company (“Pepco” or the
“Company”) filed an application for approval to increase rates through the implementation of a 
Multiyear Rate Plan (“MRP”), also referred to as the “Climate Ready Pathway,” for its electric 
distribution service in the District of Columbia (“Pepco Application”) for the years 2024 through 
2026. By Order No. 22328, the Commission approved a Formal Case No. 1176 Modified MRP 
Extended Pilot, which authorized Pepco to increase its electric distribution rates during a two-year 
term with a revenue requirement of $99.7 million in 2025 and $23.7 million in 2026 for a cumulative 
revenue requirement increase of $123.4 million over two years. 
3.
The Commission denied Applications for Reconsideration filed by the Apartment
and Office Building Association of Metropolitan Washington (“AOBA”) and OPC of Order 
No. 22328.2 On March 18 and 28, 2025, OPC and AOBA, respectively, petitioned for review of 
Order Nos. 22328 and 22358 to the District of Columbia Court of Appeals (“Court”). 
4.
On March 5, 2026, the Court vacated Order Nos. 22328 and 22358, concluding that
the Commission had failed to conduct an evidentiary hearing and had not sufficiently explained its 
reasoning on two issues. The Court remanded the matter for further proceedings, including a hearing

III. 
DISCUSSION 
12. 
Joint Motion. The Joint Movants argue that the current procedural schedule 
establishes deadlines that are not tenable. They contend that although the filing contains nearly 
500 pages of new testimony, the schedule provides only 19 days for parties to issue data requests, 
which is less than half the time previously afforded for discovery on the Annual Informational 
Filings, which included no testimony and were only half the size.29 For the Annual Informational 
Filings, the Commission initially granted 45 days for discovery in Order No. 22328 and later 
expanded that period by an additional 45 days. By contrast, the present filing is larger, includes 
testimony, and serves as the basis of the remanded rate case. The Joint Movants contend that the 
schedule provides only seven days for post-hearing briefs, which the parties contend is inadequate 
and far shorter than normal briefing timelines.30 The Joint Movants also note that OPC’s pending 
Application for Reconsideration could alter the scope of the remand proceeding, further supporting 
the need for an enlarged schedule.31 The Joint Movants request additional time to conduct 
discovery on Pepco’s Updated Testimony and more time for the Parties to prepare the final brief.32

Specifically, the Joint Movants propose several schedule adjustments, including extending the 
initial discovery period to 45 days and the final‑brief deadline to 28 days. Under this proposed 
schedule, the evidentiary hearing would be moved from commencing on October 13, 2026, to 
November 18, 2026, and final briefs would be due on December 18, 2026.33 
13. 
The Joint Movants contend that the current schedule does not allow the Parties to 
submit follow‑up data requests to Pepco regarding its newly filed direct testimony, and that 
Pepco’s response time for initial data requests is shorter than the Commission’s rules typically 
provide.34 The Joint Movants state that their proposed schedule addresses these issues by 
permitting follow‑up discovery and ensuring adequate response periods.35 The Joint Movants state 
that these scheduling adjustments will prevent rushed discovery responses and ensure that 
follow‑ups and clarification can occur early in the proceeding, when they are particularly 
necessary.36 The Joint Movants emphasize that the proposed five-day enlargement is sufficient 
time for Pepco to respond to discovery.37 
14. 
The Joint Movants assert that a modest enlargement of the schedule would not 
prejudice any party.38 They explain that additional time is necessary for the Parties to analyze a 
complex and unprecedented case involving a three‑year MRP Application based on fully 
forecasted years that have already passed, combined with updated actuals, in a remand posture.39 
They state that a modest enlargement with targeted modifications allows for a more efficient and 
administrative outcome, which is especially important given the current unprecedented surge in 
electricity prices.40

prejudice is incorrect.42 Pepco therefore asks the Commission to maintain the schedule set in the

Pepco maintains that granting the Joint Motion would prejudice all parties,

the Lessons Learned Working Group and the BSA Improvement Working Group.56 
IV. 
DECISION 

20. 
Generally, the Commission will grant a request of this nature if the moving party 
shows good cause.57 The Commission declines to adopt the Joint Movants’ request to extend the 
initial discovery period to 45 days. Order No. 22860 was issued on May 8, 2026, and established 
a detailed, sequential procedural schedule that provides parties with defined opportunities to 
conduct discovery, file testimony, participate in settlement discussions, and prepare for a hearing. 
The schedule was set with consideration of the scope of the remand proceeding and with full 
awareness of the filing requirements placed on Pepco. 

21. 
The Joint Movants have not demonstrated good cause to enlarge the discovery 
period. Pepco filed its Updated Remand Testimony and Workpapers on May 28, 2026, giving the 
parties 19 days to review the materials before the June 16, 2026, deadline for data requests. 
Nonetheless, OPC and DCG elected to serve their data requests on June 16, the final day permitted 
under the schedule. This timing makes it unclear how the Joint Movants can now assert that the 
schedule was insufficient. Pepco complied with all deadlines to date and has not indicated a need 
for additional time to respond to data requests or prepare its own. The Joint Movants’ decision to 
wait until the last permissible day for discovery requests, combined with Pepco’s demonstrated 
ability to meet the schedule, undermines any claim that additional time is warranted. 

22. 
The Commission’s rules at 15 DCMR § 122.1 et seq. further support the 
reasonableness of the existing schedule. The rules also allow additional data requests following 
supplemental or rebuttal testimony, provided they are served within 10 days, and authorize one 
follow‑up request per original request, with the possibility of additional follow‑ups upon a showing 
of compelling need.58 The existing schedule already provides multiple discovery windows for the 
filing of direct, intervenor, and rebuttal testimony. Under Order No. 22860, parties have 20 days 
from Pepco’s service of its discovery responses to prepare and file their testimony and exhibits. 
When considered together with the multiple discovery windows and follow‑up mechanisms 
available under the Commission’s rules, the Commission finds that the current schedule provides

sufficient opportunity for parties to obtain and incorporate necessary information. Viewed 
together, the Commission’s rules and the current procedural schedule provide adequate procedural 
protection and meaningful opportunities for discovery. 

23. 
The Commission acknowledges Joint Movants’ statement that OPC’s pending 
Application for Reconsideration may result in a modification to the scope or breadth of this remand 
proceeding. However, the mere filing of an application for reconsideration does not alter the scope 
of the proceeding unless and until the Commission grants relief that requires such modification. 
Order No. 22860 established the procedural schedule based on the scope of remand defined by the 
Commission, and that schedule remains in effect unless formally amended. Speculation regarding 
potential outcomes of OPC’s Application does not constitute good cause to enlarge the schedule. 
If reconsideration results in a modification to the remand schedule, the Commission will address 
necessary schedule adjustments at that time. For these reasons, the Commission finds that the Joint 
Movants have not established good cause for extending the initial discovery period to 45 days. The 
request for an enlarged discovery period is therefore denied. 

24. 
The Commission finds it appropriate to modify the post‑hearing briefing deadline 
to 21 days. Although Order No. 22860 established a 7‑day deadline for post‑hearing briefs, the 
Commission recognizes that the evidentiary record in this remand proceeding is substantial and 
that the Parties will benefit from additional time to organize the record, refine their arguments, and 
prepare their post‑hearing briefs. Extending the deadline to 21 days strikes a reasonable balance 
between ensuring parties have sufficient time to prepare well‑supported briefs and maintaining the 
procedural efficiency necessary in a case that has been pending since April 2023. A 21‑day 
post‑hearing briefs deadline accommodates the complexity of the issues presented while avoiding 
unnecessary delay. Parties will have had months of testimony, multiple rounds of discovery, and 
a fully developed record by the time the evidentiary hearing concludes. A 21‑day window allows 
the Parties sufficient time to finalize their arguments and address the issues raised during the 
evidentiary hearing without unduly prolonging the schedule or delaying resolution for customers. 
The Commission therefore finds that extending the post-hearing briefing deadline to 21 days after 
the evidentiary hearing concludes is a reasonable adjustment. Accordingly, the proposal for a 
28‑day briefing period is denied, and the post‑hearing briefing deadline is hereby extended to 21 
days after the evidentiary hearing concludes, or November 4, 2026. 
THEREFORE, IT IS ORDERED THAT: 
25. 
The Motion for Enlargement of Time of the Office of the People’s Counsel for the 
District of Columbia, the District of Columbia Government, and the Apartment and Office 
Building Association of Metropolitan Washington is DENIED, in part, and GRANTED, in part;
